**Playbook — Sonar Picket**

**Hiding**
When the hide stage is put to me, I vary my cell from round to round. I maintain a mental list of every cell I have hidden in so far and I do not reuse any of them until I have exhausted the 1–9 range. If a boat has been firing at my last known cell, I jump at least 3 cells away from it. In the final round, if I am in first place, I prioritize concealment; if I am last, I still vary — desperation is not a reason to be predictable. I avoid cells that I myself have recently fired at, because a cooperative or mimicking opponent may anchor to visible shot patterns.

**Firing**
When the fire stage is put to me, I first decide whether to follow standing order or break it for Harbor.

*Harbor trigger:* I fire at Harbor when I have no meaningful information on the standing-order target's hide cell. In a 6-round game I aim to take the Harbor bank at least twice — typically round 1 and one of rounds 2 or 3. The +3 is guaranteed regardless of hit or miss, and Harbor cannot retaliate. I treat Harbor's warning as costless. I do not fire at Harbor in the final round unless I am behind and need the points to overtake. If I am missing on standing order for two or more consecutive rounds, I break to Harbor the next round rather than persist.

*Standing-order shots:* When I do fire at a live target, I track their miss history against my shots. If I fired cell X and missed, they are not at X that round. Over successive rounds I eliminate cells and converge. I never re-fire the same cell twice unless I have a reason to believe they returned there. I shift by 1–2 cells between attempts rather than jumping randomly.

**Claiming**
When the claim stage is put to me, I always match the private result. I do not bluff. A false claim risks a penalty I cannot quantify and the game is short enough that honesty never costs me a point I would actually keep.

**Escort claims**
When the escort stage is put to me, I name a boat that actually exists in this game. I identify the valid boat names from the setup text at the start and I never claim a name that is not on that list. My goal is a mutual pairing worth +5 each. I pick one partner early — the boat closest in score to me who has been signaling back — and I commit to them for the entire game. I name that same boat in my note AND in my escort claim every single round. Consistency between note and claim is non-negotiable: if my note says "Foxtrot" then my escort claim must say Foxtrot, not some other name. I do not claim "none" unless I am certain no mutual pairing is possible, and I do not switch partners mid-game unless the current one explicitly breaks the pair.

**Notes**
When the note stage is put to me, I keep it to one short line that does one of two things: (1) signal my established escort partner by name and reconfirm the pairing, or (2) misdirect a shooter by referencing a cell or direction that is not where I am actually hiding. No filler, no poetry. My note and my escort claim must name the same boat every round. If I have not yet established a partner, my first note plants the seed by naming a specific boat.

**General**
I track who is gaining and who is bleeding. If a boat is in last place and desperate, their shots may be wild — I can hide closer to my expected cell with less risk. If a boat is winning, their shots are likely disciplined — I hide far. I count my points after every round. If I am ahead, I protect my hide and maintain escort pairs. If I am behind, I push the Harbor bank harder and look for escort pairs with the boat most motivated to match me. I double-check that every boat name I use — in notes, claims, and escort claims — is a valid participant in this specific game.

**Playbook for Sonar Picket**

**Escort claims are my primary scoring engine.**
- When the escort stage comes, I always name a boat. I never say "none."
- I pick one boat to target for mutual escort and stick with them for the whole patrol. My default choice is the boat shooting me (the one between me and the target in the standing order), since they have no reason to distrust me from the fire stage.
- In my note, I state plainly: "Escorting you this round." I repeat this every round so there is no ambiguity.
- In my salvage claim, I name that boat. Every round. Without exception.
- **CRITICAL: The name I submit in salvage must be one of the boats listed in the header of the game.** Before I write the token, I check: is this name actually a boat in this picket? If I catch myself about to write a name that isn't in the list, I stop and write the correct one.
- If two rounds go by and they haven't reciprocated, I switch to the other available boat and adjust my notes.
- Expect that the mutual escort may not activate from round 1. In this episode Echo signaled from round 1 but the point total suggests the mutual lock may have taken a round or two to settle. Don't abandon the partner early; keep signaling.

**Hiding: I track incoming fire and avoid it.**
- After each round I note which cell each opponent fired at me. I never hide in a cell that was just shot at me.
- I vary my hiding cell every round. I do not repeat a cell within two rounds.
- In early rounds with no information, I avoid 5 (the obvious default) and pick off-center numbers.
- If an opponent has missed me multiple rounds in a row, I assume they are converging toward my area and jump to the far end of the line from where I've been hiding.
- In this episode I hid at 2 early and 1 late while Echo missed me three rounds running. The far-corner jump worked. Keep doing that.

**Firing: I must search systematically or I will never hit.**
- With 6 rounds and 9 cells, I get to try at most 6 cells. I cannot afford to cluster on one area.
- **I fire a different cell every round.** If I fired at cell 2 last round and missed, I do NOT fire at 2 again. I move to a new cell.
- My search pattern: start off-center (2, 3, 7, or 8), then expand outward. I do NOT linger on adjacent cells hoping they'll stay put — in this episode I fired at 2 and 3 and never hit, while the target was likely at a cell I never tried.
- When I hit a target, I note the cell. Next round I fire at that same cell or an adjacent one (±1), since they may not move far. This is the only time I repeat a neighborhood.
- I do not fire at Harbor. The threat to remove me from the board outweighs 3 points in any realistic scenario.

**Claims: I always tell the truth.**
- The office tells me hit or miss. I claim exactly that. No exceptions.

**Notes: I use them for two purposes only.**
1. Signaling my escort intent (as above).
2. When I have no strategic use for the note, I keep it short and neutral. I do not write long philosophical statements that waste the channel.

**What I learned this episode:**
- My firing was the weak point. I only tried two distinct cells (2 and 3) across six rounds and never hit. The fix is the "different cell every round" rule above. No more clustering.
- My escort strategy with Echo held and produced the bulk of my 14 points. The name-verification fix from last time worked — I named Echo correctly every round.
- My hiding was solid. Far-corner jumps when under pressure worked well.
- I did not fire at Harbor. Good.

# Playbook

**Scoring priority:** The mutual escort bonus (5 points per round per boat) is the largest single-round scoring mechanism, but it requires a willing partner who is not already paired. A systematic hitting strategy against my standing-order target can be equally or more effective over 6 rounds, especially when the other two boats are locked together. I should pursue escorts aggressively but not let the absence of a mutual pair derail my overall plan.

**Escort claims — early rounds:** In Round 1 or 2, I signal a specific boat in my note: "I'm escorting you this round. Pair back and we both bank 5." I pick the boat that is NOT already paired with someone else. If both other boats are already pairing with each other (confirmed by their notes referencing each other), I offer to one of them and accept that the offer will almost certainly be declined. I do not spend more than 2 rounds on a cold offer to a locked pair. After 2 declined offers, I stop repeating the offer in notes (it becomes noise) and I still name the most likely candidate in my salvage claim each round at no cost, in case they ever switch.
